items.title: Yankees news: Loáisiga back; Gil, Cruz cut loose
items.author: Nick Power
items.content:
MLB.com | Bryan Hoch: As John covered yesterday morning, the Yankees have brought Jonathan Loáisiga back into the fold, securing another deal with a familiar face in the early days of free agency to augment their bullpen. The 32-year-old agreed to a two-year, $18 million contract with a club option for 2029.

Loáisiga spent eight years in pinstripes, making 193 appearances while struggling to stay healthy. He returned to form in a major way in his sole season in Arizona last year, posting a 2.42 ERA in 67 innings. The right-hander pitches off an exceptional sinker, which sat at 97.9 mph last year and helped him to an elite 55.8 percent ground-ball rate (though he uses the sinker a little less than his peak Yankees days). Loáisiga joins the re-signed David Bednar and Tim Hill as bullpen fortifications, with fellow free agent Paul Blackburn another name linked to New York.

MLB Trade Rumors | Anthony Franco: The offseason giveth, and the offseason taketh away. The Yankees parted ways with a pair of pitchers Friday, choosing to non-tender Fernando Cruz and Luis Gil. Each was projected to earn $2.3 million in arbitration. Cruz was a top late-inning option the past two seasons but suffered a partially torn UCL down the stretch last year. For the Yankees, that injury and the fact that Cruz will turn 37 in March made him expendable. For Gil, who won the AL Rookie of the Year in 2024, it was a precipitous fall from grace. Shoulder injuries and ineffectiveness limited the right-hander to 20 appearances over the past two years and, despite the fact he’s still only 28, the Yankees felt Gil no longer had a future in pinstripes.

The Yankees did tender contracts to their other six arbitration-eligible players: José Caballero, Luis García Jr., Clarke Schmidt, Anthony Volpe, Ryan Weathers and Austin Wells.

FanGraphs | Davy Andrews: The signings of Loáisiga and Hill continue the Yankees’ trend of prioritizing ground balls over strikeouts from their bullpen arms. Hill’s is an extreme case — the southpaw comfortably led baseball with a 68.8 ground-ball rate but got torched when opponents did put the ball in the air, allowing homers on nearly 31 percent of fly balls. Loáisiga’s arsenal was tweaked by the Diamondbacks last year; his four-seamer, previously an afterthought, became a viable third pitch against which opponents hit .148. He also regained speed on his fastballs, perhaps the most critical element in his resurgence.

MLB.com | Bryan Hoch: For the 15th year, Brian Cashman participated in the Sleep Out, spending a cold November night outside in a sleeping bag to raise money for Covenant House, a non-profit that provides support for unhoused youth. He does this despite the many memes it inspires of the Yankees GM sleeping on the job, telling the , “I’ll take all those shots for a good cause.” During the event, Cashman gave some updates on the free agency process, which he equates to “drinking out of a fire hose right now,” due to the rush to make acquisitions before the looming lockout. He celebrated the re-signing of Bednar and Hill to fortify the bullpen, acknowledged he’s “having conversations” about upgrading at third, and declined to anoint Spencer Jones as the presumptive starter in center.

MLB Trade Rumors | Charlie Wright: Another topic of conversation at the Sleep Out was Jasson Domínguez. Cashman noted that the Martian is “pounding the ball in winter ball,” adding that he’s been fielding calls about the 23-year-old former phenom. It remains to be seen what the Yankees GM would be looking for in an exchange for Domínguez, who has disappointed early in his MLB career but still features an enticing raw skill set. The outfielder has a 1.069 OPS with seven extra-base hits and 12 RBI in 12 Dominican Winter League games.

FanGraphs | Eric Longenhagen: FanGraphs released their updated rankings of the Yankees’ top 37 prospects Friday. The upshot is that the system is below average overall and particularly threadbare among position players. The Yankees have more promising pitching talent, as eight of the team’s top 10 prospects are hurlers. Topping the list, though, is shortstop Dax Kilby. Evaluators love the 20-year-old’s swing and defensive profile; his ascent has been slowed by injury but Longenhagen suggests a “Gunnar Henderson-esque turn” is within the realm of possibility. Carlos Lagrange and Elmer Rodríguez follow as the top pitching prospects.

FanGraphs | David Laurila: The number-28 prospect on the list, Antonio Gomez, made a fortuitous decision before the start of the 2026 season. A strong defensive catcher whose offensive profile had stalled out, the Yankees farmhand flipped to the other end of the battery. The early returns from the mound have been strong; the 25-year-old features a four-seamer sitting in the high 90s, a sinker, and a slider, with encouraging control for a recent convert. Gomez’s 16.1-inning audition between A-ball and the Arizona Fall League are enough to encourage some evaluators to now consider him a legitimate prospect.

items.title: Yankees non-tender Fernando Cruz, Luis Gil
items.author: Peter Brody
items.content:
The deadline to tender contracts to arbitration-eligible players arrived at 5pm ET on November 20th, and the Yankees have decided to non-tender Fernando Cruz and Luis Gil. The pair of right-handed pitchers become free agents, while Luis García Jr., Anthony Volpe, Ryan Weathers, Clarke Schmidt, Austin Wells, José Caballero, and Heliot Ramos have the next few months to decide whether to accept the Yankees’ offer or submit their own offers as the initial step in negotiating a salary for 2027.

Should both parties fail to agree on a number, the case would be submitted to an arbitration hearing. These hearings typically occur in February — subject to change due to the looming expiry of the CBA and expected owner lockout of the players — with the arbitration panel resolving the case by awarding the figure tendered by either the club or the player as opposed to a midpoint of those two figures.

The decision to non-tender Cruz and Gil does not come as much of a surprise. Both players were tabbed to earn $2.3 million in 2027 according to MLB Trade Rumors’ arbitration projections — an affordable amount that the Yankees nonetheless decided was better spent elsewhere given the question marks surrounding both players’ health and effectiveness going forward. It is the second year in the row that the Yankees have used the non-tender as a way to clear roster space on the pitching side. In 2025, they non-tendered five pitchers — Mark Leiter Jr., Ian Hamilton, Scott Effross, Jake Cousins, and Michael Arias — out of their 14 arbitration-eligible players.

Our own Andrés Chávez identified Gil as a non-tender candidate at the beginning of the month. It has been a precipitous fall from the stratospheric seven-start stretch that ultimately won Gil the 2024 AL Rookie of the Year Award. He has battled lat and shoulder injuries over the past two seasons, limiting him to 20 appearances (15 starts) with a 3.74 ERA, 5.44 FIP, and 58 strikeouts in 84.1 innings. An alarming loss of velocity on his fastball and worsening command has seen his strikeout rate crater from 27.3-percent between 2021-2024 to just 15.8-percent in the last two years, creating an untenable 1.9-percent strikeout-minus-walk ratio. There were question whether Gil might rediscover some effectiveness in a max-effort bullpen role, but ultimately the Yankees decided that the experiment wasn’t worth the effort. In five big league seasons with the Yankees, Gil went 21-11 in 56 appearances (51 starts), posting a 3.61 ERA, 4.54 FIP, 272 strikeouts, and 2.8 fWAR in 269.1 innings.

As for Cruz, the righty reliever became something of a cult hero thanks to his devastating splitter and enthusiastic celebrations. Arriving via trade from the Reds in the 2024-25 offseason, Cruz carved out a late-inning high leverage role by posting a 32-percent strikeout rate thanks to the splitter that allowed him to sit at the very top of the league whiff rate leaderboard. However, his appearances waned across his final two months of action in 2026, and it was subsequently revealed that he had suffered a partial tear of his UCL. The injury ended his campaign despite Cruz opting not to undergo surgery in the hope of making a late-season comeback. He was recently able to begin a throwing program, and GM Brian Cashman expressed optimism about his availability in 2027, but it appears the medicals on his elbow were scary enough to not be worth the risk at that price. In two seasons with the Yankees, Cruz made 110 relief appearances, pitching to a 3.33 ERA and 3.71 FIP with 139 strikeouts and 1.2 fWAR in 102.2 innings.

It is no surprise that the Yankees tendered contracts to the remaining seven arbitration-eligible players. The only other plausible candidate for non-tender was Schmidt, who is projected to earn $4.5 million in his third and final year of arbitration eligibility. The 30-year-old righty has missed significant parts of the last three seasons to injury — a lat strain in 2024, Tommy John surgery in 2025, and a biceps injury shortly after his return from Tommy John rehab in 2026. In total, he has made just 30 starts since the start of 2024, pitching just 164.2 innings after tossing a career-high 159 in 2023. However, Cashman confirmed that Schmidt is fully healthy entering this offseason, and the righty offers a much high floor and ceiling than Gil as starting rotation depth while also representing an intriguing multi-inning relief option.

With Cruz and Gil’s non-tenders, the Yankees have now subtracted two more arms from their already depleted relief corps. David Bednar did choose to return on the qualifying offer while the team has also reunited with Tim Hill and Jonathan Loáisiga in recent days, but there remains a good deal of work to be done to fill out the big-leaguer bullpen. There also remains the possibility that the Yankees could reintegrate Cruz and Gil on minor-league deals in the coming days.

items.title: Yankees Mailbag: The DH question
items.author: Madison Pavich
items.content:
Good afternoon everyone, it’s time to dive back into the mailbag and answer some of your questions. Remember to send in your questions for our bi-weekly call by e-mail to pinstripealleyblog [at] gmail [dot] com.

With Judge getting older and needing to stay healthy, do you see a scenario where he gets more at bats at DH this season, and at some point when Stanton has his annual muscle strain from an intentional walk, Judge is fully transitioned to DH and Stanton is released? If that doesn’t play out, how many more seasons do you see Judge playing RF?

Not right away, at least not with how the roster as constructed stands. The Yankees have their designated hitter spot locked up between Stanton, Ben Rice, and Luis García Jr. at the moment, though the team’s future with Stanton is currently cloudy at best. For now, the team is going through with bringing Stanton to spring training and seeing what he’s got left in the tank, but even removing him from the equation still leaves the position filled up with a hitter that the team wants in the lineup more often than not. There’s also been some speculation that the Yankees could turn around and flip García after acquiring him at the deadline as part of their effort to find a quality third baseman to complete the infield, shifting Rice back to first base. Rice admittedly wasn’t that good of a defender despite working with Paul Goldschmidt though, and the team certainly won’t risk moving him back behind the plate at this point with how valuable he is to the team’s offense.

Personally, I don’t think it’s worthwhile to lose García’s bat unless there’s no other avenue to upgrade third, and with the team’s incredible starting pitcher depth as well as the prospects they could part with I think there are plenty of other routes they can consider. As for Judge, while it is concerning that the last two major injuries he’s sustained have been on maximum-effort plays in the outfield (I’m still willing to consider the Dodger Stadium wall collision as more of a freak accident, but c’est la vie) he’s still a tremendous outfielder when healthy and the team would do well to maximize the value he can bring by playing him out there as long as they can. Cody Bellinger provides excellent defense in left field, but we saw how much of a struggle the other two positions were for the team on a regular basis last year, and they may not be able to find a true center fielder this offseason to improve the defense with most options for the outfield being bat-first players. I don’t know if Judge can still be Judge out there if he’s giving 80-90 percent effort out there, but his cannon arm shouldn’t be too affected by telling him to avoid a full-out dive for the ball and that change alone could be enough.

Forget rumors of Seager, Bohm, Skubal, Jeffers, etc. Boone has one year left and to spend money on long term contracts to get the same old results — start the year on fire, sleep through the summer, make the playoffs, and get bounced early — makes no sense. Why hamstring a new manager with contracts that jam the roster, let the current roster with the addition of kids or one year cheap players get through 2027, and then go crazy for 2028.

We’re making a lot of assumptions here, so let’s break this down. Aaron Boone is on a lame-duck contract, yes, but there’s no guarantee that means they’ll move on from him at the end of next year — or replace him with someone fundamentally different. If the team can’t accomplish more than another ALDS flameout three years in a row, I do think it’s unlikely that Boone gets handed another contract, but why set yourself up for failure just to move on from Boone when he’s at worst a minor part of the problem? The organization should be in win-now mode with their superstars getting up in age, and while they shouldn’t take on a bloated contract for a player that’ll only have one or two more positive years at best they should certainly be aiming to put together a World Series-caliber team instead of trusting that the kids can fill the gaps. They developed Rice and Cam Schlittler from unheralded prospect status into stardom, sure, but they made it to the majors by making the team unable to ignore them much like George Lombard Jr did this season.

Dax Kilby is a rising star in the organization but he’s still years away from the majors, and after him the rest of their top 10 prospects are all pitchers. The best-case usage of the kids in this scenario is finding smart trades to fill out the lineup, as they simply can’t all play. The only argument I’ll make in favor of not adding too much to the payroll for 2027 is that the team likely won’t be in the Tarik Skubal sweepstakes anyway and the other big ticket names don’t impress me as much, but if they were I wouldn’t hate it. Hand him a bag and the Yankees would instantly have the best rotation in baseball bar none, and still have depth to trade away to improve around the margins.

items.title: Presenting the 2026 Yankees Roster Report Cards
items.author: Pinstripe Alley Staff
items.content:
Now that we are steadily moving into the offseason with the 2026 Yankees’ disappointing ALDS loss to the Rays thankfully growing more distant to the present day, it’s time for Pinstripe Alley’s very own Roster Report Card series, where our staff evaluates and assigns grades to the most relevant players on the roster.

This series is scheduled to begin in mid-October and run through early December, skipping only Thanksgiving and weekends. We’ll start with the free agents who are imminently likely to hit the market and then proceed alphabetically. Missing from this series are Yankees manager Aaron Boone and general manager Brian Cashman, but you can find their evaluations by visiting the highlighted links.

As a reminder, the writer for a specific player isn’t assigning their own grade; these grades are averaged from our entire staff’s submissions.

items.title: Yankees Birthday of the Day: Clark Griffith
items.author: Kevin Winterhalt
items.content:
Though Clark Griffith is the first man to manage the New York baseball team we now call the Yankees, his time in New York is merely one chapter in a story of one of the giants of baseball’s early history. That’s no shot at Griffith’s time in New York and his importance to the franchise. It’s just he had such an amazing life and career.

He was already an accomplished hurler when he came to New York and became the player-manager of the club, in its first season in The Big Apple. And long after he hung up his cleats, he remained an integral part of baseball in the first half of the 20th century.

November 20, 1869 (Clear Creek, MO) October 27, 1955 (Washington, DC) 1903-07 (player/manager), 1908 (manager)

Clark Griffith was already a grizzled veteran when American League President Ban Johnson named him manager of the New York Highlanders (often called the Americans in the press) prior to the 1903 season. It was the inaugural campaign for the club, which relocated from Baltimore after the Orioles folded following two seasons.

The diminutive Griffith (listed at 5-foot-6) was a right-handed pitcher, and a good one, at that. Between 1894 and 1901, he won at least 20 games in a season seven times. His first season in New York was also his last one as a starting pitcher, and he tossed more than 200 innings while managing the club to a disappointing fourth-place finish.

Griffith’s pitching days were not over, however. He transitioned to the bullpen and continued to pitch at a high level while trying to steer the Highlanders to a pennant. In 1904 and 1906, he came close, with the club finishing in second place each season, mere games from wining the American League.

Modern Yankee fans are used to skipper Aaron Boone getting himself tossed from games, though he was shockingly well-behaved in 2026. He’s far from the first Yankee manager to get the hook, of course. Griffith, by virtue of being the first manager, gets that honor. Like his modern successor, Griffith also got himself suspended for his conduct toward umpires.

On Monday, August 27th, 1906, Griffith took umbrage with a safe call at first base while playing St. Louis. As a result, the umpires ordered Griffith off the field. The Highlanders’ skipper took his sweet time about it. Unfortunately for him, AL President Johnson was in the crowd, and the next day he suspended Griffith indefinitely. Yeesh. “Savages in the Box,” this was not. Seems a little harsh. But wait — there’s more. The indefinite suspension might have something to do with Griffith fighting umpire Tim Hurst earlier in the season, which also got him suspended. For that round of fisticuffs, Griffith received a five-day suspension. His ban in August lasted a week.

The Highlanders bottomed out on Griffith’s watch in 1908, and in June he decided it was time for him to move on. Owner Frank J. Farrell tried to dissuade the disheartened Griffith, but to no avail.

“It was fighting against fate,” Griffith told , “And I knew when I had enough. I do not know who my successor will be, but I understand [Kid] Elberfeld is mentioned for the place. If that is so, I wish him the best of luck, and I hope my successor will pull the team out of the rut and place them where they belong.”

Griffith’s warm feelings for the club definitely did not last forever. At his death, the noted, “Mr. Griffith had two pet dislikes in his lifetime. One was John McGraw and the other was the New York Yankees.”

Griffith’s time in baseball was by no means done when he left New York. Most famously, he eventually found himself in Washington, where he leveraged his assets to obtain a 10 percent stake in the notoriously bad Senators. “First in war; first in peace, and last in the American League,” the old saying went.

Griffith won five pennants in nine years before again relying on his assets to buy a majority share in the franchise. By 1920, he’d transitioned out of the dugout and into the owner’s box, ending a 20-year managerial career where he won 1,491 games (26th most all-time). In 1924, his Senators finally won the World Series, upsetting the New York Giants. They would win further pennants in 1925 and 1933 as well.

Clark Griffith is almost certainly the most important person in the history of Washington baseball, with all due respect to Walter Johnson. He’s also the answer to an obscure yet important bit of trivia. Who was responsible for the tradition of US presidents throwing out the first pitch? It was Griffith, who in 1910 asked President William Howard Taft to toss out the first ball. Taft obliged and the rest is history.

Griffith was also key to baseball’s relationship with the U.S. government and military during both world wars. In World War I, he organized an initiative to get baseball equipment for every American soldier overseas. He even got President Woodrow Wilson to chip in. During World War II, he was one of the people who helped convince President Franklin Roosevelt to keep baseball playing.

He’s the only man in baseball history to have played, managed, and owned a team for at least 20 years each. Clark Griffith was elected to the Major League Baseball Hall of Fame in 1946. His Senators would eventually pass to his son, Calvin, who would move them to Minnesota in 1961 to become the Twins (and become rather infamous in his own right).

Clark Griffith died on October 27, 1955, in Washington, D.C. In its obituary for the legend, noted what former president Harry S. Truman had said about Griffith in 1946 when he had thrown out a presidential first pitch, the tradition Griffith started decades earlier.

“Mr. Griffith is a shining example of what this great country of ours can produce.”

Happy birthday to the Yankees’ first skipper.

See more of the “Yankees Birthday of the Day” series here.

items.title: Yankees 2026 Roster Report Cards: George Lombard Jr.
items.author: Jonathan Farrar
items.content:
Few positions, or the players manning them, have been debated as intensely as shortstop for the New York Yankees over the last several seasons. Heading into 2026, many fans hoped the club would find a way to move on from the Anthony Volpe experience. However, the club made no external moves and started the season with José Caballero slotted in at the position as the team waited for a rehabbing Volpe to return.

Along the way, injuries and performance, both struggles by the incumbents and red-hot play in the minors, led the Yankees to hand the reins at shortstop over to 21-year-old George Lombard Jr. The rookie would spend August, September, and October at shortstop for the Yankees in what really is the throne of NYC. 

In terms of how it went, the staff here at PSA averaged out to a B-minus. In academic speak, that would mean Lombard understood the core material and performed above average, but did not master the assignment.

42 G, 166 PA, 23 R, 36 H, 4 2B, 1 3B, 7 HR, 22 RBI, 2 SB, .237/.285/.414, 92 OPS+, 93 wRC+, 0.4 fWAR, 1.1 bWAR.

Pre-arbitration eligible.

Before reaching the show, Lombard was on an absolute tear in the minors. Starting the season in Double-A, he hit .312 with a .971 OPS in 20 games, which earned him a ticket to Scranton. Lombard’s season looked like it might be coming off the rails after an adjustment period, and then he sprained two fingers, which sidelined him for a month and caused him to miss the MLB Futures Game. However, he came back in mid-July and forced the Yankees’ hand right before the Trade Deadline, going on a 14-game heater to the tune of a .377 average, .477 OBP, and 1.081 OPS.

On August 4th, after surviving the Trade Deadline himself, and with the Yankees not acquiring an outside option at shortstop, the club called Lombard up to the show. The kid finished the minor league season slashing .284/.411/.498 with 12 home runs. This performance led Baseball America to name him the Yankees’ Minor League Player of the Year for 2026.

Lombard’s 2026 season at the professional level, and the basis for our grading, really is a story of three parts. The first was a euphoric honeymoon stage. Lombard committed just one error in his first 14 games and racked up eight Defensive Runs Saved (DRS) in his first 100 innings, looking like a potential Platinum Glove winner. This all came as he homered in his first pro at-bat and slashed .320/.393/.560 with a .953 OPS across his first 25 at-bats. It was too good to be true.

After the rise came the fall, as Lombard slumped with the glove and bat. In late August, Lombard made the wrong kind of history, committing an error in six straight games and tying a 105-year-old franchise record. With the stick, big league pitchers started getting him to chase and roll over breaking balls, causing his average to sink to .217 by mid-September. The vibes from some fans really went from “next” to “next Volpe.”

To the kid’s credit, he righted the ship down the stretch and saved himself in the third act. From September 9th through the end of the regular season, Lombard’s defense stabilized to league average, and he hit five home runs in his final 16 games. He carried that confidence into the postseason, going 3-for-4 in the Wild Card opener against Boston and finishing October batting .333 (6-for-18), albeit with an error in the ALDS.

I’ll save the hype train for future preview articles. However, despite only having an 86 mph average exit velocity, Lombard finished the season pacing for 27 home runs over 162 games. There’s also a lot of room for growth, as Lombard had a 17.3 percent walk rate at Triple-A and only a six percent rate in the majors through his first 42 games, or essentially a quarter of a season. The defense, especially when playing beside a big league-quality third baseman, was fine for someone who was just a few months into being able to buy an adult beverage.

Lombard’s minor league season was an A+, while his rookie season comes in at a B-. With some growing pains behind us and a few more likely ahead, here’s to hoping Lombard can continue to improve and develop into a difference-maker. What grade would you circle in red for Lombard’s 2026 season, and what do you predict he’s produce next season?

See more of the Yankees Roster Report Card series here.

items.title: Yankees sign Jonathan Loáisiga to two-year deal
items.author: John Griffin
items.content:
So far this winter, the bullpen has been a clear priority for the Yankees, who saw no fewer than four important relievers from the 2026 season become free agents. After re-signing Tim Hill and bringing back David Bednar on the qualifying offer, the team has now made its third addition to the bullpen, coming to terms with old friend Jonathan Loáisiga on a two-year deal with a team option for 2029.

Canal 4 News in Loáisiga’s native Nicaragua had the news late last night, the man himself hinted at it with a picture of the NYC skyline on his Instagram story, and Jorge Castillo of ESPN confirmed it this morning. MLB.com’s Mark Feinsand reported the total outlay of the contract as $18 million across the two years and buyout.

Yankees fans are, of course, very familiar with the man nicknamed Johnny Lasagna. Signed as a minor-league free agent in 2016 after a couple years in the Giants’ organization, Loáisiga spent parts of eight seasons with the big league club, and served as the bullpen’s ace fireman/setup man in 2021 and the second half of 2022. Injuries and ineffectiveness plagued the right-hander for the next three seasons, however, and after a lackluster 2025, the Bombers declined his team option for 2026.

It turned out to be the best thing for him. After sitting on the market for most of the winter, Loáisiga signed a minor-league free agent deal with the Diamondbacks last January. He made the team out of spring training, stayed healthy for a full season for the first time in five years, and put together one of the best seasons of his career, posting a 2.42 ERA in 67 innings. Perhaps more importantly, his advanced metrics were some of the best of his career, and helps explain why there were so many suitors for the recently-turned 32-year-old (the Mets, Phillies, Dodgers, and Blue Jays were all reportedly in on him).

Despite the small time apart, though, Loáisiga is not exactly the same pitcher who Yankee fans remember. Gone are the days where he threw the sinker like Mariano Rivera threw the cutter, i.e., pretty much every pitch. Although it’s still his main offering (he threw it 35 percent of the time last year), that is a far cry from the 54-to-69-percent usage rates from his first Yankees stint; in its stead, he’s upped his changeup, fastball, and cutter.

While nobody would ever consider Loáisiga a strikeout pitcher, these changes oversaw a slight bump in strikeout percentage to 18.4 percent from his 16.6-percent rate between 2022-24 and a slight drop in walk rate to a career-best 5.0 percent, all without sacrificing ground-ball rate. The question will just be how his body holds up after an actual full, healthy season.

Even with Loáisiga, Hill, and Bednar back in the fold, the Yankees are probably not yet done looking at bullpen arms — assuming they ever truly feel like they have enough bullpen arms. At this point, though, the Yankees have successfully turned it from a “need” to a “want,” as they’re no longer so thin out there that Yerry De los Santos and Angel Chivilli were listed as two of the team’s higher-leverage relief arms on the FanGraphs Depth Chart.

One could, of course, absolutely still argue that they still need a big swing-and-miss arm in the ’pen, as they’re still lacking in that regard and not everyone should be a pitch-to-contact guy. As we wait for the league to come to a screeching halt in 10 days due to the owners’ insistence on a lockout, getting some things crossed off the winter to-do list is certainly not a bad thing, and Loáisiga checks another box.

items.title: MLB, college sports, and the sports propaganda moment
items.author: John Griffin
items.content:
When we’re in school, we hear a lot about propaganda. American history textbooks show us political cartoons from the late 19th and early 20th century about the abolition of slavery, the rise of industrial robber-barons, and the progressive movement. European art historians discuss how Louis XIV used paintings and sculptures to present himself as the “Sun King” as he strengthened the power of the French crown over the First and Second Estates. In my own Roman history classes, I spend multiple weeks demonstrating how the emperors employed literature, history, sculpture, and construction projects to assert the supremacy of both Rome and the imperial household. Whether in middle school, high school, or college, students regularly grapple with propaganda in their history classes, learning how people with access to communicative resources have been able to present their own version of reality to sway public opinion in their favor.

Once we’re out of school, though, propaganda falls by the wayside, and ceases to be a concern. It exists, in the public consciousness at least, not as a part of our lives, but as a historical oddity, the behavior of a bygone era — or, when it’s acknowledged in the modern world, as something that happens in the nebulous “over there,” not “here.” And yet, what else can we call the flood of political advertisements in every commercial break that made the World Series borderline unwatchable if not propaganda? After all, are they not trying to sell their version of reality, as opposed to that of their opponents, in an effort to sway voters?

Propaganda is most often understood in terms of politics, but it doesn’t have to be. And right now, we’re living in what I call a sports propaganda moment, as two major entities — the NCAA and Major League Baseball — have gone on the figurative warpath, spending millions of dollars in advertising not to get people to watch their product, but to generate outrage from fans on their own behalf against that of their players.

Whether you’re a fan of a power conference school who competes for the national championship every year or a small liberal arts college who celebrates when their team gets blown out during the March Madness tournament because that meant they made it in the first place, you’ve almost certainly been exposed to commercials sponsored by the Saving College Sports organization in support of the Protect College Sports Act. Since the start of the 2026 college football season (and in truth, since last bowl season, as commercials in support of the bill ran even before it was officially introduced in Congress back in June), they have run a massive ad campaign encouraging fans to contact their congressional representatives and pressure them to vote yes on the bill. Backed by multi-million athletic programs and employing household names such as Deion Sanders and Nick Saban (a current coach and a former one, respectively), these ads center the conversation about the bill on the legitimate concerns fans have about today’s Wild West NIL era — namely, the constant transfers — while ignoring the fact that the bill attempts to, as much as legally possible, reassert the extreme levels of control that the conferences and schools used to have over their athletes.

Starting in the middle of the summer, Major League Baseball has rolled out their own ad campaign in preparation for the upcoming lockout, which is now just a week and a half away. Focused on MLB.tv and social media, the “Level the Playing Field” campaign directly argues for the implementation of a salary cap and floor, claiming that the league cannot have competitive balance due to the payroll disparities that exist between small- and large-market teams. These ads ran all summer, during the All-Star Game festivities, the postseason, the World Series, and the awards season. While, ironically, this meant that the league plastered everywhere a chart in which the team with the second-highest payroll, the Mets, missed the playoffs as the team with the second-lowest payroll, the Rays, won the pennant, the very fact that the league spent time and energy publicly fighting the players during what should be the biggest annual celebrations of the sport is a testament to their priorities — and the important role that these ads played in their pre-lockout preparations.

Now, obviously, these two situations aren’t 100 percent comparable. Decades of corruption and a refusal to negotiate common sense solutions with its players forced college athletes to turn to the courts for assistance, and once the courts got involved, federal involvement and oversight was all but guaranteed, and all the political machinations that entails. Major League Baseball, meanwhile, is attempting, for the second time this decade, to use the expiration of the Collective Bargaining Agreement as an opportunity to break the power of the players’ union and implement the salary cap that they believe will see franchise values skyrocket. Sure, the almighty dollar may be the driving force for both the NCAA and MLB — both the Protect College Sports Act and the salary cap are, at their core, attempts to rein payrolls in and ensure cost certainty — but each organization is so fundamentally different from the other that their financial systems are incomparable.

Nonetheless, the fact that both collegiate athletics and professional baseball have adopted the same tactic, large-scale propaganda campaigns meant to turn the fans against the players, reflects the unique historical moment we are in. As we saw during the last CBA negotiations, social media has allowed players to interact with fans directly, allowing them to, for example, directly argue against the league’s propaganda, much like Jameson Taillon did last week.

Last time around, this direct connection between players and fans appeared to help the players in the negotiations, as the players were able to successfully mock the league’s insistence on removing all evidence of players’ likenesses on all media. That being said, should there be a disconnect between the fans and the players, this has the potential to backfire on the players, and perhaps this is what Major League Baseball is going for here. Baseball may be in the midst of a renaissance, but that doesn’t mean the fans don’t think that some things need to be fixed. Deferred money, especially when done to the extent the Dodgers have in recent years, has been regularly mocked in baseball-related online spaces. The rise of gambling has resulted in real, concrete ethics concerns. Blackouts, TV restrictions, and an ever-increasing stable of required streaming services have made watching the games a veritable chore. Solving none of these problems requires a salary cap, and yet, the league has tried to use their media machine to tie all of them to it, to limited success. In fact, it may have backfired just a bit: the frequency with which they have said “this proposal is contingent on the players accepting a salary cap” has sparked quite a bit of mockery online.

Of course, what has sparked such a large push for a cap at this time is the fact that this CBA negotiation might be the league’s best guaranteed opportunity for one in the foreseeable future. The Dodgers and the Mets have giftwrapped the league two bogeymen to use to sway fans to their side in the negotiations: between the former’s willingness to exploit deferred money and their acquisitions of Shohei Ohtani, Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Rōki Sasaki, Blake Snell, Kyle Tucker, Edwin Díaz, Tanner Scott, Tyler Glasnow, Teoscar Hernández, and Tarik Skubal over the last three years, and the latter’s willingness to ignore all luxury tax thresholds and common sense to sign whatever hot free agents they can, there’s quite a bit of ammunition to turn fans of small- and medium-market teams against the owners. The Players’ Association, meanwhile, has been in a bit of disarray this year, with Tony Clark one of several union executives shown the door within the last 12 months; while it’s unclear whether this will actually harm the union in negotiations, turmoil at the top can at least give the impression of weakness to an ownership group looking to make major gains.

Together, these scenarios have things ripe for Major League Baseball to push all their chips to the center of the table and try to get their salary cap, as it might be their best opportunity for a while. And so, the propaganda machine spins on.

items.title: Today on Pinstripe Alley – 11/20/26
items.author: Madison Pavich
items.content:
We’re less than a week away from Thanksgiving now, and the Yankees have started to get a bit active before the holidays kick in. After locking down David Bednar’s contract for 2027, there were overnight musings that Jonathan Loáisiga reportedly is coming back to New York after a year away in Arizona. His 2026 season was excellent, and it was also the first healthy season he’d had in a while, but up until now it seemed like there was more interest from the Dodgers or Mets than the Yankees. If they managed to get a hometown discount for their former reliever then they might’ve gotten away with a bit of a steal, but we’ll have to wait and see what the actual details of this potential deal are.

We’ve got a few things in store for you today, beginning with John giving us his thoughts on MLB’s early PR propaganda laying the ground for their side of the upcoming lockout. Jonathan hands out our latest report card to the rookie George Lombard Jr. after his whirlwind second half with the big league team, Kevin remembers the legacy of one of baseball’s early titans in Clark Griffith, and then in the afternoon I’ll be back to answer your latest mailbag questions.

1. If the Yankees have Jonathan Loáisiga back in the fold, how many games do you expect to see him in next year?

2. Do they still need another established reliever in your mind, or do you trust Brian Cashman and Matt Blake to make due from here?

items.title: Yankees news: MLB continues to frolic with private equity
items.author: Joshua Diemert
items.content:
Front Office Sports | Ben Horney: After the Yankees reached an investment deal with Apollo Global Management over the summer, the rapacious claws of private equity continue to sink into what was once the great American pastime. Swiss firm Seidler Equity Partners bought out an as-yet-undisclosed stake in Rawlings, the official baseball supplier to MLB, that the league has owned since 2018. MLB did say they would maintain “meaningful ownership” of the company, but it seems Seidler is the controlling partner. Expect offense to rise once the ghouls learn rubber is cheaper than leather.

NJ.com | Adam Zagoria: The Yankees have reportedly been in contact with Randy Arozarena’s camp, as the mercurial outfielder courts offers in his first true taste of free agency. The Yankees’ struggle from the right side of the plate was a story from the moment Aaron Judge went down, and in those dog days of summer where it felt like they faced a left-handed starter four out of five days, right-handed power would be an excellent add to the roster, and Randy’s never had a bad year at the plate. His defense and baserunning though…

Yahoo! Sports | Jackson Kruse: The Yankees made a small splash yesterday, inking switch-hitting outfielder Allan Castro to a minor league deal. Castro, just 23, became a minor-league free agent after playing in the Red Sox system since 2019, was a little underwhelming with an 88 wRC+ in 119 games for Triple-A Pawtucket, but per FanGraphs boasts above average power both raw and in-game. If the Yankees can build some kind of contact profile, he might end up a surprising depth piece going forward.
